title: Isaac Inherits the Promise and Peace
summary: In famine Isaac stays in the land, repeats his father’s deception, prospers under God’s blessing, yields over disputed wells, and receives peace at Beer-sheba.
historicalContext: Chapter 26 is the only chapter devoted chiefly to Isaac as head of the family. A second famine strikes the semiarid south, and Isaac moves from the Negeb to Gerar, a royal town in the coastal plain ruled by a king bearing the dynastic name Abimelech. Decades separate these events from Abraham’s dealings with an earlier Abimelech, so the treaty and the wells of chapter 21 now belong to a new generation that has quietly forgotten them. Life for a seminomadic herdsman depended on wells, pasture, and the goodwill of settled rulers. Isaac had no rights as a resident alien, and a wealthy household of flocks, herds, and servants could look like a political threat. The setting explains the envy, the stopped wells, the quarrels between herdsmen, and the formal visit of the king with his counselor and army commander seeking a sworn covenant at Beer-sheba.
literaryContext: Placed between Esau’s sale of the birthright (25:29–34) and the stolen blessing (chapter 27), this chapter shows the heir of the promise living under God’s blessing without scheming for it. Its scenes deliberately retrace Abraham’s path: famine, a divine word about the land, a wife called a sister, conflict and covenant with Abimelech, wells, and the naming of Beer-sheba. The phrase “Abraham thy father” recurs, and the structure moves from promise at Gerar through conflict over wells to promise and peace at Beer-sheba. The repetition proves that the covenant has passed intact to the second generation, while Isaac’s fearful lie proves that the promise rests on God’s faithfulness. The closing note about Esau’s Hittite wives opens the following story and contrasts the son who follows his father with the son who disregards him.
themes: The Abrahamic promise confirmed to Isaac
Obedience to God’s law before Sinai
Meekness that makes room for peace
Choices that grieve a covenant home

outline.title: Promise in the Time of Famine
outline.summary: The LORD forbids Isaac to go to Egypt, confirms the oath sworn to Abraham, grounds it in Abraham’s obedience, and Isaac stays in Gerar.

outline.title: Rebekah Called a Sister
outline.summary: Isaac repeats his father’s deception, Abimelech discovers the truth, rebukes him, and places the couple under royal protection.

outline.title: Blessing That Breeds Envy
outline.summary: Isaac reaps a hundredfold and grows very great, the Philistines stop Abraham’s wells, and Abimelech sends him away.

outline.title: Wells, Room, and an Altar
outline.summary: Isaac reopens his father’s wells, yields at Esek and Sitnah, finds room at Rehoboth, and receives a night promise at Beer-sheba.

outline.title: Covenant and the Well of the Oath
outline.summary: Abimelech seeks a sworn covenant, Isaac feasts with him and sends him away in peace, and water is found at Shebah.

outline.title: Esau’s Hittite Marriages
outline.summary: Esau marries two Hittite women, and they bring bitterness of spirit to Isaac and Rebekah.

verses.bibleText: And there was a famine in the land, beside the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went unto Abimelech king of the Philistines unto Gerar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Famine had already shaped the story of the promise once. Soon after Abram entered Canaan, hunger drove him down to Egypt, where fear led him to hide his marriage (12:10–20). The narrator now speaks of a famine “beside the first famine,” a careful note that this is a new crisis in a new generation. The recurrence is deliberate. Isaac will walk through a set of trials remarkably like his father’s, and the reader is meant to watch whether the son will respond as Abraham did at his best or at his worst.

Isaac had been living near Beer-lahai-roi in the dry Negeb (25:11), a region that suffers first when the rains fail. Gerar lay to the northwest, nearer the coast, where the land was more fertile and a royal city might have stored grain. It also sat on the route toward Egypt, which depended on the Nile rather than on rainfall. Isaac’s move to Gerar may have been the first stage of a journey southward, a reasonable plan for a herdsman with many mouths to feed.

The ruler of Gerar is called Abimelech, “king of the Philistines.” Many decades had passed since Abraham’s treaty with a king of that name (21:22–34), so this is most naturally a successor bearing a royal or dynastic name, much as “Pharaoh” served in Egypt. The Philistines of this period were an early group of settlers in the southwest, distinct in setting from the later Philistine cities of the judges and kings.

The verse ties the chapter to the one before it. Esau had just traded his birthright for a meal because he felt himself starving (25:29–34). Now Isaac faces real hunger on a larger scale, and the question is whether the bearer of the promise will trust God for bread in the land God has given.

wordNotes.explanation: The word describes severe scarcity of food, usually caused by failed rains. In Genesis famine repeatedly tests the patriarchs and moves the story forward, from Abram’s descent to Egypt to Joseph’s rise there. It becomes a setting in which God’s provision and the faith of His people are both brought into view.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD appeared unto him, and said, Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This is the first time Scripture records that the LORD appeared to Isaac. Until now he had stood in the shadow of his father, a son received by promise, laid on the altar at Moriah, and given a wife through the faithful search of Abraham’s servant. At the moment of crisis God speaks to him directly, and the heir of the covenant becomes a recipient of revelation in his own right.

The first word is a prohibition: “Go not down into Egypt.” Egypt represented the obvious, sensible refuge in famine, and Abraham had gone there with painful results. Abraham had also been determined that Isaac should never leave the land of promise, insisting that his servant must not take the young man back to Mesopotamia (24:6–8). God now confirms that conviction. Isaac’s calling is bound to Canaan, and leaving it, even for good practical reasons, would cut against the purpose God was working out.

The positive command recalls Abram’s first call. Abram was told to go “unto a land that I will shew thee” (12:1); Isaac is told to dwell “in the land which I shall tell thee of.” The son must live by the same kind of trust as the father, not knowing every detail in advance but relying on the God who directs each step. Obedience here meant choosing to remain in a hungry land on the strength of a word.

The pattern reaches far beyond Isaac. Israel would later be warned not to return to Egypt for help (Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 31:1), and the call of faith still involves refusing the refuges that seem safest when God has spoken otherwise.

The command was also a gift. God did not leave Isaac to weigh the options alone in a time of crisis. He spoke, and in speaking He removed the uncertainty that might have driven Isaac toward the same mistakes his father made in Egypt.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּרָא אֵלָיו יְהוָה (vayyera’ ’elayw YHWH) — the LORD appeared unto him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is the passive or reflexive form of “to see,” meaning God made Himself seen. The same expression marks the LORD’s self-revelation to Abram at the start of his life in Canaan, linking Isaac’s experience with his father’s. The LORD takes the initiative; revelation is His gift, not a human achievement.

verses.bibleText: Sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee, and will bless thee; for unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give all these countries, and I will perform the oath which I sware unto Abraham thy father;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Sojourn in this land” calls Isaac to live as a resident alien in territory he does not yet possess. The Hebrew verb describes someone who stays among others without the rights of a citizen, depending on their tolerance. There may also be a wordplay with the name Gerar, the very place where Isaac was to sojourn. Remaining there in famine would require him to trust God rather than the visible security of Egypt’s granaries.

To this command God attaches a cluster of promises. First comes “I will be with thee,” a promise of presence that becomes a keynote in the lives of Isaac and Jacob (26:24; 28:15) and later sustains Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:12). For a man without legal protection among strangers, God’s presence was his only real security. Then comes “and will bless thee,” the same blessing first spoken to Abram (12:2).

The gift of land is enlarged in its wording: “all these countries.” The plural looks beyond the single region of Gerar to the many territories held by the peoples of Canaan, all of which would one day belong to Isaac’s descendants. The promise did not depend on Isaac’s political strength; it rested on God’s commitment.

That commitment is named plainly: “I will perform the oath which I sware unto Abraham thy father.” After Moriah the LORD had sworn by Himself (22:16–18). An oath made by God cannot fail, because there is no one greater by whom He could swear (Hebrews 6:13–18). Isaac’s future therefore rested on a promise already ratified. His obedience would be the way he entered into its enjoyment, not the foundation that held it up. The New Testament draws on this same unchanging oath to anchor the hope of believers who flee to Christ for refuge.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to live as a stranger or resident alien, without the standing of a native. The patriarchs are repeatedly described this way in Canaan, and Hebrews takes up their sojourning as a picture of faith that looks for a city God has prepared. The cognate noun gēr later shapes Israel’s laws protecting the stranger.

wordNotes.term: וְאֶהְיֶה עִמְּךָ (ve’ehyeh ‘immekha) — and I will be with thee
wordNotes.explanation: This first-person promise of presence is new in the patriarchal promises at this point and becomes central for Isaac and Jacob. Its form echoes the self-revelation of God to Moses as the One who will be with His people. In the New Testament it reaches its fullest meaning in Emmanuel, “God with us.”

verses.bibleText: And I will make thy seed to multiply as the stars of heaven, and will give unto thy seed all these countries; and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Three promises given to Abraham are now repeated to Isaac almost word for word. The image of descendants as numerous as “the stars of heaven” comes from the night when Abram believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness (15:5–6), and it was confirmed with an oath at Moriah (22:17). The land, “all these countries,” is promised again. Finally comes the universal promise: “in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.”

This last promise lifts the covenant beyond family and territory. From the first call of Abram, God’s purpose embraced “all families of the earth” (12:3). Through one chosen line He intended to bring blessing to every people. The repetition to Isaac shows that this worldwide purpose did not end with Abraham. It passed to the son of promise rather than to Ishmael, just as it would pass to Jacob rather than Esau.

The “seed” in this verse is first a collective word for Isaac’s many descendants, as the comparison with the stars shows. Yet within the same promise the word narrows toward a single descendant through whom the blessing reaches the nations. Paul presses this point when he notes that the promise speaks of “seed,” singular, and identifies that Seed as Christ (Galatians 3:16). Peter announced the same fulfillment to the crowd in Jerusalem, declaring that God had raised up His Servant Jesus to bless them by turning them from their iniquities (Acts 3:25–26).

The blessing of the nations, then, is not finally prosperity or territory. It is the gift of righteousness and the Spirit through faith in Christ (Galatians 3:8–9, 14). Isaac, hungry in Gerar, was carrying a promise whose reach extended to the ends of the earth, and the line that would produce the world’s Redeemer was being guarded through his fragile household.

wordNotes.term: וְהִתְבָּרְכוּ בְזַרְעֲךָ (vehitbarakhu vezar‘akha) — and in thy seed shall … be blessed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb form can be read as “shall be blessed” or “shall bless themselves,” meaning the nations will seek and find blessing through Abraham’s line. Either way, Isaac’s seed becomes the channel of God’s blessing to the world. The Greek Old Testament renders it passively, and the New Testament follows that sense when it quotes the promise.

The noun can mean offspring in the collective sense or a single descendant. Here it first refers to Isaac’s numerous posterity, yet the promise keeps open a narrower focus on one particular descendant. Paul draws on that singular sense to identify Christ as the Seed through whom the nations are blessed.

verses.bibleText: Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God explains why He is repeating the promise: “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice.” The same wording closed the oath at Moriah (22:18), when Abraham did not withhold his only son. Abraham’s life had been marked by prompt response to God’s word, from leaving Haran (12:4) to rising early to journey to the mountain (22:3). The blessing now passing to Isaac is linked to the faithfulness of the father.

The verse then describes that obedience with four terms: Abraham “kept my charge,” together with God’s “commandments,” “statutes,” and “laws.” These are the very words Moses would later use to urge Israel to keep the covenant given at Sinai (Deuteronomy 11:1). Their appearance here, centuries before Sinai, shows that God’s will was already known and obeyed. The law did not begin with Moses. Long before the tables of stone, God had made His moral requirements known, and Abraham walked in them. The command to walk before God and be perfect (17:1), the practice of circumcision, the offering of tithe to Melchizedek (14:20), and the instruction of his household to keep “the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment” (18:19) all belong to this obedience. Cain’s guilt, Joseph’s horror of adultery as sin against God, and the Sabbath sanctified at creation (2:2–3) and known before Sinai (Exodus 16:23) point the same direction. The Ten Commandments expressed afresh at Sinai a moral law that already governed God’s people.

This verse does not teach that Abraham earned the covenant. God called him by grace while he was still among idolaters (Joshua 24:2–3), and Abraham believed God before he had done any of these works (15:6; Romans 4:3). His obedience was the shape his faith took. James draws exactly this connection: Abraham’s faith worked together with his works, and by works his faith was made complete (James 2:21–23). Faith without obedience would be empty; obedience without faith would be mere effort.

The word to Isaac carries an implied call. The blessing came to him through a father who trusted and obeyed; he too must hear God’s voice and keep His charge if he is to enjoy what was promised. The same holds for every child of Abraham by faith. Jesus links love for Him with keeping His commandments (John 14:15), and the redeemed at the end are described as those who keep God’s commandments and hold the faith of Jesus (Revelation 14:12).

wordNotes.term: מִשְׁמַרְתִּי מִצְוֹתַי חֻקּוֹתַי וְתוֹרֹתָי (mishmarti mitsvotay chuqqotay vetorotay) — my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws
wordNotes.explanation: The four nouns together express the full range of God’s requirements. Mishmeret is what one is charged to guard; mitsvot are specific commands; chuqqot are fixed ordinances; torot are instructions or laws. The string reappears in Deuteronomy for the covenant law, which shows that what Abraham kept was God’s revealed will already before Sinai, not a later invention.

The expression means “as a consequence of” or “on account of.” It ties the blessing to Abraham’s obedience as its visible occasion, while the earlier oath grounds it in God’s own commitment. The same phrase marks Abraham’s response at Moriah.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac dwelt in Gerar:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The response is told in three Hebrew words: “And Isaac dwelt in Gerar.” No speech, no protest, no bargaining. God had said not to go down to Egypt, and Isaac did not go. Where Abraham’s faith was displayed by going out, Isaac’s is displayed here by staying put. Remaining in a famine-stricken region on the strength of a promise was an act of trust, and the narrator records it without embellishment.

The simplicity of the note also prepares for contrast. Isaac obeyed the command about place, yet the next verse shows that his trust had limits when danger touched him personally. Obedience in one area does not guarantee faithfulness in every area, and Scripture presents the patriarchs honestly, with their strengths and weaknesses side by side.

Gerar was not the place Isaac might have chosen for the long term. It was a foreign king’s territory, and he had no claim to any of it. Yet God had said “this land,” and Isaac accepted the limits of the word he had received. Faith often begins this way, with a single act of compliance before the full shape of God’s provision is visible. The harvest of verse 12 was still a season away.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to sit, settle, or remain. It answers the divine command to dwell in the land and shows Isaac’s compliance. The same verb later describes Jacob dwelling in Canaan, the land of his father’s sojournings, linking the generations in their response to the promise.

verses.bibleText: And the men of the place asked him of his wife; and he said, She is my sister: for he feared to say, She is my wife; lest, said he, the men of the place should kill me for Rebekah; because she was fair to look upon.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Almost immediately after receiving the promise “I will be with thee,” Isaac acts as though he must protect himself. When the men of Gerar ask about the woman with him, he answers, “She is my sister.” The narrator lets us hear his inner reasoning: he feared that saying “my wife” would cost him his life, “because she was fair to look upon.” Rebekah’s beauty, first noted when the servant met her at the well (24:16), now becomes in Isaac’s mind a source of danger.

The parallels with Abraham are unmistakable. Twice Abraham had presented Sarah as his sister for the same reason (12:11–13; 20:2, 11). Yet Isaac’s lie was worse in one respect. Sarah was in fact Abraham’s half-sister (20:12), so his statement was a dangerous half-truth. Rebekah was Isaac’s cousin’s daughter, not his sister in any sense the men of Gerar would have understood. Isaac had no partial truth to shelter behind.

The failure is sobering because of its timing. Isaac had just heard God’s voice, had obeyed by staying in the land, and had been assured of divine presence and protection. The same man who once lay on the altar at Moriah, trusting his father and his father’s God, now could not trust that God to guard his marriage. Faith in the large decisions of life does not automatically extend to the daily pressures that touch personal safety.

The repetition also shows how patterns pass from one generation to the next. Whether Abraham had told his son about his own lapses is not recorded, but the son reached for the same strategy under the same kind of fear. Inherited weaknesses explain much about human behavior, yet Scripture never treats them as an excuse; each person answers for his own choices (Ezekiel 18:20). Only grace breaks such cycles, and the rest of the chapter shows God’s faithfulness to a son who did not deserve it.

wordNotes.term: אֲחֹתִי הִוא (’achoti hi’) — she is my sister
wordNotes.explanation: Isaac uses exactly the words of Abraham in Gerar a generation before. The verbal echo invites comparison: the son repeats the father’s strategy. Unlike Sarah, Rebekah was not related to Isaac as a sister even by a half relationship, so the claim had no element of truth.

wordNotes.term: טוֹבַת מַרְאֶה (tovat mar’eh) — fair to look upon
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase, literally “good of appearance,” was used of Rebekah when Abraham’s servant first saw her. It recalls the description of Sarah in Egypt and explains the fear of both patriarchs. What God had given as a gift becomes in a fearful mind a reason for self-protective deceit.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when he had been there a long time, that Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and, behold, Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator notes that Isaac “had been there a long time” before the deception unravelled. That detail exposes how groundless his fear had been. Months or perhaps years passed, and no one in Gerar had attempted to take Rebekah or to harm Isaac. The danger he imagined never materialized; the lie only created a different risk.

Discovery came through ordinary means. Abimelech happened to look out of a window and saw Isaac “sporting with Rebekah his wife.” In the earlier episodes God intervened directly, with plagues on Pharaoh’s house (12:17) and a dream to the first Abimelech (20:3). Here no dream or plague is needed. Providence works through a glance from a palace window, and the truth comes to light without miracle.

The word translated “sporting” is a play on Isaac’s own name, which means “he laughs.” It describes affectionate behavior between husband and wife that no brother and sister would display. There is gentle irony in the scene: the man whose name recalls joyful laughter (21:6) gives himself away through the very playfulness his name suggests. Marital love, rightly expressed, cannot easily be hidden, and the covenant bond Isaac tried to conceal proved itself in an unguarded moment.

The narrator does not explain why Isaac let his guard down that day, and the point is not his carelessness. A deception built on denying a marriage could not be kept up forever. Truth about the deepest relationships of life tends to show itself, and God used that ordinary reality to bring Isaac’s fearful scheme to an end before it caused real harm.

wordNotes.explanation: This intensive participle comes from the verb “to laugh,” the root of Isaac’s name. In context it denotes intimate caressing between spouses. The same form was used of Ishmael’s mocking at Isaac’s weaning feast, so the word carries different shades by setting; meaning must be decided by context rather than by the root alone.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech called Isaac, and said, Behold, of a surety she is thy wife: and how saidst thou, She is my sister? And Isaac said unto him, Because I said, Lest I die for her.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech summoned Isaac and confronted him directly: “Behold, of a surety she is thy wife: and how saidst thou, She is my sister?” The king had seen enough to be certain. His question is not idle curiosity but moral protest; he expects an explanation from a man who had misled his people.

Isaac’s reply is brief and self-centered: “Because I said, Lest I die for her.” He offers no apology and makes no attempt to justify the lie by any principle. His concern had been his own survival, with no thought for Rebekah’s honor or for the guilt he might bring on others. The pronouns tell the story: “I said … lest I die.” Fear had narrowed his vision to himself.

The scene places the heir of the promise in an awkward position. A Philistine king is the one asking the moral question, and the man who walked with God has no good answer. The covenant people are often humbled by the integrity of outsiders, and Scripture records such moments so that God’s people will not imagine that privilege excuses dishonesty (Romans 2:24). Isaac’s confession at least has the merit of honesty now; the truth, once spoken, opens the way for correction.

Abimelech’s question also shows the king taking marriage seriously. He did not shrug off the lie as a harmless precaution. To him the difference between a sister and a wife mattered, because it determined how every man in Gerar ought to treat Rebekah.

wordNotes.term: אַךְ הִנֵּה (’akh hinneh) — behold, of a surety
wordNotes.explanation: The particle ’akh adds emphasis, here expressing certainty, while hinneh calls attention to what has been seen. Together they convey Abimelech’s conviction that the truth is now undeniable. The king is not guessing; he states what his own eyes have confirmed.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“What is this thou hast done unto us?” Abimelech’s rebuke echoes the question God asked Eve in the garden (3:13) and the words Pharaoh and the earlier Abimelech used with Abraham (12:18; 20:9). Once again a ruler outside the covenant line speaks with moral clarity to a patriarch. The words “unto us” matter: Isaac’s lie had endangered an entire community.

The king explains the danger. “One of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife.” The Hebrew suggests something that could easily or almost have happened. Had any man in Gerar, believing Rebekah unmarried, taken her, he would have committed adultery unawares, and the whole people would have shared the guilt. Abimelech understood that sin against marriage was not a private matter. It brought culpability before God on the community where it occurred.

This sense of guilt shows that knowledge of God’s moral law was not confined to Abraham’s family. The sanctity of marriage, rooted in creation (2:24), was recognized even among the peoples of Canaan, and adultery was seen as a grave wrong. Later Israel would receive detailed teaching about guilt and the guilt offering (Leviticus 5:14–19), and the commandment against adultery would be written in stone (Exodus 20:14). Abimelech’s instinct anticipates both.

The verse also exposes a principle that reaches beyond this story. Deception does not only wrong the one deceived; it can lead others into sin they never intended. Isaac’s fear for himself had made him careless of the souls of his neighbors. The people of God are called to walk in such a way that they put no stumbling block before others (Romans 14:13), and to bring blessing rather than guilt to the communities where they live.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes guilt incurred by wrongdoing and the liability to make reparation for it. In Leviticus the same word names the guilt offering. Abimelech recognizes that adultery, even committed unknowingly, would bring guilt on the whole people. Isaiah later uses the term for the Servant who gives His life as an offering for guilt.

The adverb means “almost,” “nearly,” or “easily.” It conveys how close the community came to serious sin. The KJV “lightly” captures the sense that it could have happened with little difficulty and without anyone realizing the wrong being done.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech charged all his people, saying, He that toucheth this man or his wife shall surely be put to death.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech moved from rebuke to protection. He issued a royal decree to all his people: “He that toucheth this man or his wife shall surely be put to death.” The verb “touch” covers both sexual approach to Rebekah and any violence against Isaac. The very danger Isaac had feared was now removed by public law, and the couple who had no rights as foreigners found themselves under the king’s explicit protection.

The outcome reveals the grace of God at work through unexpected means. Isaac had tried to protect himself with a lie and only created a hazard. God protected him through the conscience and authority of a pagan ruler. The promise “I will be with thee” (26:3) was fulfilled in spite of Isaac’s failure, not because of his cleverness. The psalmist would later sing of God reproving kings for the sake of the patriarchs and saying, “Touch not mine anointed” (Psalm 105:14–15).

The solemn penalty, “shall surely be put to death,” uses the same doubled expression as God’s warning in Eden (2:17). Life and death hang on respect for what God has joined together. The decree guarded more than one household; it preserved the marriage through which the line of promise, and ultimately the Messiah, would come.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb naga‘ means to touch or reach, and in context includes harmful assault and sexual contact. The earlier Abimelech was told that God had kept him from touching Sarah. Here the decree extends that protection to Isaac’s household by royal command.

wordNotes.term: מוֹת יוּמָת (mot yumat) — shall surely be put to death
wordNotes.explanation: The doubled verb intensifies the penalty, marking a capital offense. The idiom becomes standard in the Mosaic law for grave crimes, including adultery. Its use here shows how seriously the violation of marriage was viewed even outside Israel.

verses.bibleText: Then Isaac sowed in that land, and received in the same year an hundredfold: and the LORD blessed him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then Isaac sowed in that land.” The patriarchs were primarily herdsmen, moving with their flocks, yet Isaac also planted crops. The fertile soil around Gerar made this possible, and it marks Isaac as the patriarch most rooted in the land. In a time of famine, when others feared to plant, Isaac put seed into the ground in the place God had told him to stay.

The harvest was extraordinary: “an hundredfold” in the same year. In that region a yield of thirty or fifty times the seed sown would be considered very good. A hundredfold represents the upper limit of fruitfulness, and it came in a season of drought. The narrator leaves no doubt about the reason: “and the LORD blessed him.” The harvest did not come from Isaac’s farming skill or from the soil alone. It was the direct outworking of the promise “I will … bless thee” (26:3).

The contrast with the previous verses is striking. Isaac had just failed through fear and deception, yet God’s blessing did not depart from him. Divine favor rested on the man because of the covenant, not because of his flawless record. The blessing confirmed that Isaac had been right to stay in the land rather than go down to Egypt. Faith that obeys God’s word about where to live finds that God provides where He has placed His people.

Jesus would later speak of seed falling on good ground and bringing forth “some an hundredfold” (Matthew 13:8, 23). In the parable the abundant harvest belongs to the one who hears the word and understands it. Isaac’s field illustrates the same principle in physical form: abundance comes from God, and it is given to those who trust His word enough to sow where He has sent them.

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase, literally “a hundred measures,” describes a yield a hundred times the seed sown. The Greek Old Testament read the consonants slightly differently as “barley,” producing “barley a hundredfold,” but the Hebrew points to the scale of increase. The image signals maximal fruitfulness given by God.

verses.bibleText: And the man waxed great, and went forward, and grew until he became very great:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator piles up words for growth: Isaac “waxed great, and went forward, and grew until he became very great.” The Hebrew repeats the verb “to be great” three times, and the expression “went forward” conveys steady, continuing increase. His prosperity was not a single good harvest but a sustained rise over time.

The language recalls the promise to Abram, “I will … make thy name great” (12:2), and the description of Abraham as “very rich” (13:2). It also echoes what the servant told Laban about his master: “the LORD hath blessed my master greatly; and he is become great” (24:35). The son now stands where the father stood. The promises did not weaken in passing to the second generation; Isaac became as great as Abraham.

Such greatness was a gift and a test. It displayed God’s faithfulness to all who watched, yet it would also stir hostility, as the next verse shows.

Moses later warned Israel that prosperity in the land could tempt them to say, “My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17). The narrator guards against that reading of Isaac’s rise by tying it directly to the blessing of the LORD in the preceding verse. Isaac’s greatness was received, not manufactured.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּלֶךְ הָלוֹךְ וְגָדֵל (vayyelekh halokh vegadel) — and went forward, and grew
wordNotes.explanation: The verb “to go” paired with an infinitive expresses continuing or progressive action, “he kept on growing.” The construction stresses steady, sustained increase. A similar idiom describes David growing stronger while the house of Saul grew weaker.

verses.bibleText: For he had possession of flocks, and possession of herds, and great store of servants: and the Philistines envied him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac’s wealth is itemized in the measures of his world: “possession of flocks, and possession of herds, and great store of servants.” Sheep, goats, cattle, and a large household of workers made him a significant presence in the region. In a society where power was tied to people and livestock, such a household could rival a small town.

The result was envy: “and the Philistines envied him.” The same blessing that displayed God’s favor also provoked resentment. The pattern recurs throughout Scripture. Joseph’s brothers envied him (37:11), the rulers of Egypt grew fearful as Israel multiplied (Exodus 1:7–10), and the chief priests handed Jesus over out of envy (Mark 15:10). Envy cannot bear to see another blessed and seeks to diminish what it cannot share.

The Philistines had already witnessed God’s favor on Isaac. They could have recognized it, as their king eventually would (26:28), and sought peace and blessing through him. Instead they resented him. The promise that the nations would be blessed through Abraham’s seed did not force anyone to receive that blessing; it could be welcomed or resisted. Envy closes the heart to what God is doing in another person’s life.

For God’s people the verse carries a double warning: blessing does not guarantee peace with neighbors, and envy toward those whom God has blessed is itself a sin to resist (James 3:16; 1 Peter 2:1).

wordNotes.term: וַיְקַנְאוּ אֹתוֹ (vayqanne’u ’oto) — and they envied him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb qana’ can express jealousy, zeal, or envy depending on context. Here it is the resentful envy of those who see another prosper. The same verb describes Rachel envying Leah and Joseph’s brothers envying him. Envy sets the stage for hostile actions that follow.

verses.bibleText: For all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Envy turned into sabotage. The narrator steps back to explain that the Philistines had stopped up all the wells Abraham’s servants had dug, filling them with earth. These wells had been the subject of a sworn agreement between Abraham and the earlier Abimelech at Beer-sheba (21:25–31), when Abraham gave seven ewe lambs as a witness that he had dug them. Now that Abraham was dead, the Philistines ignored that covenant and made the wells useless.

In the dry south, water was life. A herdsman without wells had to move his flocks or watch them die. Filling the wells with earth did not destroy the underground water, but it made the wells unusable until someone took the trouble to dig them out again. The act was a way of saying that Abraham’s family had no claim to this territory and was not welcome to stay.

The verse also shows how quickly agreements can be forgotten once the people who made them are gone. Abraham had secured his rights through a covenant, but the next generation of Philistines did not honor it. Isaac inherited not only his father’s blessings but also the consequences of his neighbors’ broken faith.

Spiritually, stopped wells have often served as a picture of truth and blessing obscured by neglect or hostility. What God once provided through faithful forebears can be buried by later generations. Isaac’s task, which follows, would be to reopen what had been closed.

The narrator’s parenthesis also prepares for verse 18. Before Isaac can reopen the wells, the reader must know who closed them and why. The stopped wells stand as evidence that the treaty of Abraham’s day had been betrayed, and they explain why Isaac’s labor in the valley carried both practical and symbolic weight.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb satam means to stop up, block, or close. Stopping wells was a recognized act of hostility in warfare, as when Israel stopped the wells of Moab. Here it signals the Philistines’ rejection of the earlier treaty and their attempt to drive Isaac away.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech said unto Isaac, Go from us; for thou art much mightier than we.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Finally Abimelech spoke openly: “Go from us; for thou art much mightier than we.” The king who had protected Isaac by royal decree now asked him to leave. The reason was political. Isaac’s household had grown so large that the Philistines felt threatened by it. A prosperous foreigner living in their midst seemed a danger to their own security.

The words “much mightier than we” anticipate the anxiety of a later Pharaoh, who said of the Israelites in Egypt, “the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we” (Exodus 1:9). The blessing of multiplication, promised to Abraham and now visible in Isaac, provoked fear in rulers who could not control it. Readers in Moses’ day, hearing this account on their way out of Egypt, would recognize the pattern.

Isaac did not resist the king’s request. He had the strength to dispute, yet he chose to leave. That decision would set the course for the rest of the chapter, in which Isaac repeatedly yields and God repeatedly makes room.

The request also marks a turning point in Isaac’s relationship with Gerar. The protection of verse 11 had shielded his person and his marriage, but it did not secure his place among the Philistines. Royal favor proved temporary. The only security that lasted through the chapter was the presence God had promised.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb ‘atsam means to be strong, numerous, or mighty. It is the same root used of Israel’s multiplication in Egypt, which aroused Pharaoh’s fear. Isaac’s growth thus prefigures the nation’s growth and the hostility it would provoke.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac departed thence, and pitched his tent in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac obeyed the king’s request without argument. He “departed thence, and pitched his tent in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there.” The move was not a great distance; he withdrew from the city itself to the broad wadi from which Gerar took its name. He kept his household within the region God had told him to stay in, while removing himself from the immediate presence of those who resented him.

The phrase “pitched his tent” is telling. Isaac had sown fields and grown great, almost settling like a townsman, but now he is again a tent-dweller. The verb is the one later used for Israel encamping on its journeys through the wilderness. The patriarchs lived in the land of promise “as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles” (Hebrews 11:9), and Isaac’s return to the tent reminds the reader that the inheritance had not yet come.

None of the patriarchs fought for the land. They trusted God to give it to their descendants at the proper time (15:13–16). Isaac’s quiet withdrawal expresses that same trust and models the meekness Jesus would bless (Matthew 5:5).

The location still lay within reach of Gerar’s officials, close enough for the old wells of Abraham to be within his range. Isaac had stepped back without stepping out of the land God had assigned him, keeping both the peace his neighbors demanded and the obedience God required.

wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes a wadi, a valley with a seasonal stream that runs after rains and often holds water beneath its bed. Such valleys were natural places to dig wells. The valley of Gerar thus offered Isaac a reasonable hope of finding water away from the city.

The verb chanah means to encamp or set up a temporary dwelling. It is the characteristic verb for Israel camping during the exodus journey. Its use here stresses Isaac’s unsettled, pilgrim life in the land not yet possessed.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham his father; for the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham: and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
In the valley Isaac began by digging out the wells his father had dug. The narrator repeats the explanation: the Philistines had stopped them “after the death of Abraham.” While Abraham lived, the treaty held; once he was gone, hostility surfaced. Isaac’s first act was not to look for new sources but to recover the old ones, reclaiming what had already been provided.

Then he “called their names after the names by which his father had called them.” In the ancient world naming a well established a claim to it, much as a deed does today. By restoring the original names Isaac declared that these wells belonged to Abraham’s family by right and by covenant. He was also honoring his father’s memory and the history of God’s provision at those sites. Each name preserved a testimony to what God had done for Abraham.

Here is a picture of faithful continuity. Isaac did not try to make a reputation by inventing something new. He reopened what his father had opened and kept the names his father had given. There is a lesson here for every generation of believers. Truths God revealed to faithful people in the past can be buried by neglect, opposition, or the passage of time. Restoring them is not a step backward; it is a recovery of living water. Jeremiah urged his people to ask for “the old paths, where is the good way,” and to walk in them (Jeremiah 6:16).

The work was laborious. Filled wells had to be dug out by hand, basket by basket. Isaac’s willingness to invest that effort showed his conviction that what God had given his father was worth recovering. The wells would sustain his household, and their restored names would remind all who drew from them of the God of Abraham.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּשָׁב יִצְחָק וַיַּחְפֹּר (vayyashov Yitschaq vayyachpor) — and Isaac digged again
wordNotes.explanation: The verb shuv, “to return,” combined with another verb expresses doing an action again. Isaac “returned and dug,” reopening what had been closed. The idiom underscores restoration rather than new construction, recovering his father’s wells.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac's servants digged in the valley, and found there a well of springing water.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Beyond the old wells, Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and struck something better: “a well of springing water.” The Hebrew calls it “living water,” meaning water that flows from an underground spring rather than collecting in a cistern from rain. In a dry land such a source was a prize, giving a steady supply in every season.

The discovery was another sign of God’s blessing. Isaac had been forced from the city and had lost the use of his father’s wells, yet in the place of exile God gave him a spring. What looked like loss became provision.

The phrase “living water” gathers rich meaning in later Scripture. Through Jeremiah the LORD called Himself “the fountain of living waters,” rebuking His people for hewing out broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13). Jesus offered the Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well living water that would become in the one who drinks “a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:10–14), and He invited the thirsty at the feast to come to Him and drink (John 7:37–38). The springs Isaac found in the valley point forward to the inexhaustible life God gives through His Son.

The servants’ success is also a quiet commentary on the Philistines’ strategy. They had tried to drive Isaac out by denying him water. God answered by giving him water of a better kind than the wells they had blocked. Human hostility can close one source, but it cannot shut the hand that opens the springs of the earth (Psalm 104:10).

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase, literally “living water,” describes fresh, flowing spring water as opposed to still water in a cistern. In the law it designates running water required for certain purifications. The prophets and Jesus use the image for the life that comes from God Himself.

verses.bibleText: And the herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is our's: and he called the name of the well Esek; because they strove with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The new spring immediately became a point of conflict. “The herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac’s herdmen, saying, The water is our’s.” The claim was a bald assertion of ownership over water Isaac’s men had found and dug. It recalls the strife between the herdsmen of Abram and Lot (13:7) and the earlier dispute over a well seized by Abimelech’s servants (21:25). In a land where water meant survival, such quarrels were bitter and frequent.

Isaac named the well “Esek,” meaning “contention,” “because they strove with him.” He did not fight for it. He gave the place a name that recorded what had happened and moved on. The name served as a memorial, not of Isaac’s rights but of the hostility he encountered.

Isaac had grown great enough to defend his claim; the king himself had admitted he was mightier than the Philistines (26:16). Choosing not to press that advantage required restraint. The Lord’s servant must not strive but be gentle toward all (2 Timothy 2:24), and Paul urges believers, as far as it depends on them, to live peaceably with everyone (Romans 12:18).

Isaac’s conduct also reflects the long patience of God’s people in the land of promise. The patriarchs owned no more of Canaan than a burial cave and a few wells. They held the promise by faith and declined to seize by force what God would give in His own time. Isaac’s meekness at Esek was faith in action. Even the losses were recorded in faith. To name a well is to remember it, and Isaac left behind a memorial of wrong suffered without revenge.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is explained by the related verb “they strove” (hit‘asseqû) in the same verse. It means contention or dispute and occurs only here in the Old Testament as a name. By naming the well this way, Isaac turned the site into a memorial of the quarrel.

The verb riv means to contend, quarrel, or bring a legal complaint. It describes the herdsmen’s dispute over the water. The same verb names the place where Israel later quarrelled with Moses over water, Meribah.

verses.bibleText: And they digged another well, and strove for that also: and he called the name of it Sitnah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac’s servants dug another well, and the quarrel broke out again: “they … strove for that also.” Isaac named this one “Sitnah,” a word expressing hostility or accusation. The two names, Esek and Sitnah, form an escalating pair: the first records a dispute, the second open opposition. The Philistines were not merely contesting a single well; they were resisting Isaac’s presence altogether.

Again Isaac did not retaliate. He accepted the loss and let the name stand as testimony. A man who could twice give up a hard-won source of water without violence was showing remarkable trust that God would provide elsewhere. Such patience is not passivity. It is the strength of one who knows that his inheritance is secure in the hand of God and need not be grasped by force.

The repeated loss would have been costly. A new well required days of labor, and every surrender meant moving flocks and households again. Isaac’s restraint therefore cannot be dismissed as indifference. He felt the injustice, as the names show, yet he chose to bear it rather than turn his servants into combatants. Peter would describe Christ in similar terms: when He suffered, He threatened not, but committed Himself to the One who judges righteously (1 Peter 2:23).

wordNotes.explanation: The name means hostility, opposition, or accusation. A related noun appears in Ezra for a written accusation against the returned exiles. The word shares a root with satan, “adversary,” but here it describes human opposition, not a spiritual being; context, not etymology, governs the meaning.

verses.bibleText: And he removed from thence, and digged another well; and for that they strove not: and he called the name of it Rehoboth; and he said, For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac “removed from thence” once more and dug yet another well. This time “they strove not.” He had moved far enough from Gerar that the Philistine herdsmen made no claim. At last he could draw water in peace. He called the place “Rehoboth,” meaning “broad places” or “room,” and gave his reason: “For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.”

The sequence of names tells a story: contention, then hostility, then room. Isaac’s patience was rewarded, not by winning the disputes but by being led beyond them. He attributed the outcome to God alone. It was not his strength, his diplomacy, or the exhaustion of his opponents that brought the change; “the LORD hath made room.” The verb Isaac used is the very verb from which the name Rehoboth comes.

The second half of Isaac’s declaration, “we shall be fruitful in the land,” echoes the blessing of creation, “Be fruitful, and multiply” (1:28), renewed to Noah (9:1) and promised to Abraham’s line (17:6). Isaac saw in Rehoboth a token that God’s original purpose for humanity would be worked out through his family in the land God had given them.

The psalmists often speak of God bringing them into “a large place” after distress (Psalm 18:19; 118:5). The image fits Isaac’s experience. Hemmed in by envy and conflict, he found that God could open space where human opposition had closed it. The site is often identified with Ruheibeh, some twenty miles southwest of Beer-sheba, where large ancient wells have been found.

Rehoboth stands as an encouragement to all who suffer for refusing to fight for their own rights. Those who leave their cause with God discover that He knows how to make room for His people (Psalm 4:1). Meekness does not mean losing the inheritance; it is the path by which the meek inherit the earth (Psalm 37:11).

wordNotes.explanation: The name means “broad places” or “wide spaces,” and it is explained by the verb hirchiv, “he has made room,” in the same verse. The pairing ties the name directly to God’s act of enlarging Isaac’s space. A city of the same name appears earlier in the list of nations.

wordNotes.term: הִרְחִיב יְהוָה לָנוּ (hirchiv YHWH lanu) — the LORD hath made room for us
wordNotes.explanation: The causative verb means to make wide or to enlarge. Psalms use the same verb for God relieving distress by giving room, as in “thou hast enlarged me when I was in distress.” Isaac acknowledges that the space came from God, not from his own effort.

verses.bibleText: And he went up from thence to Beer-sheba.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac did not remain at Rehoboth. “He went up from thence to Beer-sheba,” a journey of some twenty miles northeast into slightly higher ground. Beer-sheba held deep associations for his family. Abraham had dug a well there, made a covenant with the first Abimelech, planted a tamarisk, and called on the name of the LORD, the everlasting God (21:31–33). It was also where Abraham had lived after returning from Moriah (22:19), and it was likely the home of Isaac’s youth.

The move brought Isaac back to the place where his father’s worship had been centered. What happened there that very night shows that the move was providential.

The verb “went up” fits both the geography and the spiritual movement of the narrative. Isaac had been driven from place to place by the hostility of others. Now he went up of his own accord to the site of his father’s altar. The story has moved from Gerar, where Isaac lied in fear, through the valley of disputed wells, to the place of worship. Restoration often follows this kind of path, back to the place where God was first known.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb ‘alah means to ascend or go up. It is used for travel to higher ground, and in Scripture often for going up to a place of worship. Beer-sheba lay on rising ground compared with the coastal region of Gerar.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD appeared unto him the same night, and said, I am the God of Abraham thy father: fear not, for I am with thee, and will bless thee, and multiply thy seed for my servant Abraham's sake.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The LORD appeared unto him the same night.” The timing is significant. Isaac had just arrived at Beer-sheba after a season of envy, expulsion, and repeated disputes. He had yielded again and again. Now, on the first night in the place of his father’s altar, God came to him with reassurance. It is the second recorded revelation to Isaac, and it frames the chapter: God spoke to him at the beginning in Gerar (26:2) and speaks again at the end in Beer-sheba.

God introduced Himself as “the God of Abraham thy father.” This is the first time the title appears in this form. It identifies the LORD by His relationship with Abraham, a relationship begun when God called Abram out of an idolatrous family (Joshua 24:2–3). The God who had walked with Abraham now pledged Himself to Isaac. Jesus would later appeal to this very title to prove the resurrection: God calls Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and “he is not a God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). Though Abraham was resting in the grave, the covenant God remained committed to him and would raise him up.

“Fear not” addresses the anxiety that had shaped Isaac’s life in Gerar. He had feared for his life and lied to protect himself; he had faced hostility and repeated loss. God speaks to that fear with the same words He spoke to Abram after the battle with the kings (15:1). The remedy for fear is the promise of presence: “for I am with thee.”

The blessing is then restated: “and will bless thee, and multiply thy seed for my servant Abraham’s sake.” The phrase “for … Abraham’s sake” shows that the promise rested not on Isaac’s merit, which had just been compromised, but on God’s covenant with his father. Abraham is called “my servant,” a high title given later to Moses, David, and supremely to the Servant of Isaiah’s prophecies. God’s faithfulness to one servant spills over in blessing to his descendants, foreshadowing the way blessing comes to believers for the sake of the obedient Servant, Christ (Isaiah 53:11; Romans 5:19).

wordNotes.explanation: This prohibition with the verb “to fear” is a frequent divine reassurance in Scripture. It is first spoken to Abram after his battle and later to Jacob, to Israel through the prophets, and by angels at the birth of Christ. It is always grounded in God’s presence or promise.

The title “servant of the LORD” is a mark of honor given to those whom God has chosen and commissioned. Applied to Abraham here, it is later given to Moses, David, and the messianic Servant in Isaiah. It describes belonging to God and acting on His behalf.

verses.bibleText: And he builded an altar there, and called upon the name of the LORD, and pitched his tent there: and there Isaac's servants digged a well.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac responded to God’s appearance with three actions. First, “he builded an altar there.” This is the only altar Scripture attributes to Isaac, and it stands at the place where his father had worshiped. Altars in Genesis mark the places where God has met His people and where they respond with sacrifice and devotion. Abraham built altars when he entered the land and wherever God appeared to him (12:7–8; 13:18). Isaac now follows in that pattern.

Second, he “called upon the name of the LORD.” The expression first appears in the days of Seth (4:26) and describes public worship, prayer, and proclamation of God’s name. Abraham had called on the name of the LORD at Beer-sheba (21:33). Isaac continues the worship of his father in the same place, making it his own.

Third, he “pitched his tent there.” Worship came first; settling came after. The order matters. Isaac’s household would live in the presence of the altar, and his tent would stand where God had met him. In the same way, worship is meant to shape the life of every household, not to be added on after other priorities are fixed.

Finally, “there Isaac’s servants digged a well.” The material needs of the household were met in the place of worship. The altar and the well stand side by side, a picture of the God who meets both the spiritual and physical needs of His people. Jesus taught His disciples to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, with the promise that daily needs would be added (Matthew 6:33). Isaac’s order of life at Beer-sheba anticipates that teaching.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּבֶן שָׁם מִזְבֵּחַ (vayyiven sham mizbeach) — and he builded an altar there
wordNotes.explanation: The noun mizbeach comes from the verb “to slaughter” and denotes a place of sacrifice. Building an altar acknowledged God’s appearance and dedicated the site to His worship. The patriarchal altars anticipated the sacrificial system and, through it, the one sacrifice of Christ.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְרָא בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה (vayyiqra’ beshem YHWH) — and called upon the name of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase signifies invoking God in prayer and worship and may include public proclamation of His name. It links Isaac with Seth’s line and with Abraham’s worship at the same site. Paul echoes the expression in describing salvation through calling on the Lord.

verses.bibleText: Then Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ahuzzath one of his friends, and Phichol the chief captain of his army.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene shifts abruptly. Abimelech, who had asked Isaac to leave, now comes to him at Beer-sheba. He does not come alone. With him are “Ahuzzath one of his friends, and Phichol the chief captain of his army.” The presence of both a senior counselor and the commander of the army signals an official embassy. This is not a social call but a diplomatic mission between two powers.

“Friend” in this setting is a court title for the king’s closest adviser, comparable to Hushai, “David’s friend” (2 Samuel 15:37). Phichol bears the same name as the army commander who accompanied the earlier Abimelech to Abraham (21:22). Since nearly a century separates the two treaties, the name is most likely a title or a recurring family name rather than the same individual.

The journey itself is a reversal. The king who had sent Isaac away now travels to him. The one who had said “Go from us” now seeks Isaac’s favor. Proverbs describes this very pattern: when a man’s ways please the LORD, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7).

Isaac’s willingness to meet them at all is also notable. He had been wronged repeatedly, yet he did not refuse the delegation or send it away unheard. The next verses show that his openness was neither naive nor resentful.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun rea‘ ordinarily means companion or neighbor, but “the king’s friend” was an official title for a trusted counselor at court. Ahuzzath’s presence shows the formal, high-level character of the delegation. Solomon’s court also had an officer called the king’s friend.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac said unto them, Wherefore come ye to me, seeing ye hate me, and have sent me away from you?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac greeted the delegation with understandable suspicion: “Wherefore come ye to me, seeing ye hate me, and have sent me away from you?” He named the hostility plainly. The Philistines had envied him, stopped his father’s wells, contested his new ones, and expelled him from their city. He had every reason to wonder what they wanted now.

Isaac’s question was honest without being vindictive. He did not list every grievance or demand compensation. He simply asked why those who had driven him away now sought him out. Peace that ignores past wrongs entirely is shallow, and Isaac’s frankness opened the way for an honest agreement. Yet he did not refuse to meet with them. His question left the door open for reconciliation, and the rest of the scene shows him walking through it.

Jesus taught that if a brother sins against you, you should tell him his fault (Matthew 18:15). Isaac’s directness, combined with his willingness to listen, reflects that principle in seed form.

The exchange also exposes the instability of the Philistine position. Their hostility had been driven by envy and fear, not by any wrong Isaac had done. Now that the same fear made them seek a treaty, Isaac was entitled to ask what had changed. The answer would come from their own mouths.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb sane’ ranges from active hatred to rejection or setting aside. Here it describes the Philistines’ hostility shown in their actions. Jephthah uses a similar complaint when the elders who had expelled him came seeking his help.

verses.bibleText: And they said, We saw certainly that the LORD was with thee: and we said, Let there be now an oath betwixt us, even betwixt us and thee, and let us make a covenant with thee;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech’s answer is remarkable: “We saw certainly that the LORD was with thee.” Using the covenant name of Israel’s God, the Philistine king acknowledged what had happened. The blessing on Isaac was not luck or skill. God’s presence had made the difference. The promise of 26:3, “I will be with thee,” had become visible even to outsiders.

The evidence lay in Isaac’s prosperity during famine, his survival after expulsion, and his repeated success in finding water where others contested him. A herdsman driven from royal pastureland should have been ruined. Instead he flourished. Abimelech concluded that it was wiser to be at peace with such a man than to remain his enemy.

His proposal was formal: “Let there be now an oath betwixt us, even betwixt us and thee, and let us make a covenant with thee.” The oath was a solemn pledge invoking curse on any who broke it, and the covenant set out the terms of the relationship. The repetition “betwixt us, even betwixt us and thee” shows how earnestly the king sought binding commitment.

The scene shows the promise to Abraham coming to fulfillment in miniature. God had said that the nations would be blessed through Abraham’s seed (26:4) and that He would bless those who blessed Abraham (12:3). Here a foreign king, recognizing God’s favor on Isaac, seeks to align himself with it. The pattern points forward to the day when nations would come to the light of God’s people (Isaiah 60:3) and take hold of a Jew’s garment, saying, “We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you” (Zechariah 8:23). It reaches its fullness in Christ, through whom Gentiles who were far off are brought near (Ephesians 2:12–13).

wordNotes.term: רָאוֹ רָאִינוּ (ra’o ra’inu) — we saw certainly
wordNotes.explanation: The infinitive followed by the finite verb intensifies the statement: “we have clearly seen.” It expresses conviction based on unmistakable evidence. Abimelech is not speculating; he is affirming what was obvious to all.

The noun denotes a sworn agreement that carries a self-imposed curse should one party break it. It differs from a simple promise by its solemn sanctions. The term is used for the oath with which Abraham’s servant was bound and for the curses attached to covenant breaking.

verses.bibleText: That thou wilt do us no hurt, as we have not touched thee, and as we have done unto thee nothing but good, and have sent thee away in peace: thou art now the blessed of the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech spelled out the terms: “That thou wilt do us no hurt.” The powerful Philistine king was asking a tent-dwelling herdsman for protection. That alone shows how far the situation had changed. Isaac had become the stronger party, and Abimelech recognized it.

The king then described his own conduct in flattering terms: “as we have not touched thee, and as we have done unto thee nothing but good, and have sent thee away in peace.” The claim was selective. It was true that no one had physically harmed Isaac, thanks to the royal decree. But the Philistines had stopped his wells, quarrelled over his new ones, and expelled him. Isaac’s peaceful departure was the result of his own restraint, not the king’s generosity. Abimelech was retelling the past to make his request more palatable.

Isaac did not dispute the account. He let the king’s version stand without correction. There is wisdom in knowing when not to press a point. Having named the hostility honestly in verse 27, Isaac now chose peace over the satisfaction of winning an argument. Love “thinketh no evil” and does not keep a ledger of wrongs (1 Corinthians 13:5).

The king ended with an acknowledgment that outweighed his self-justification: “thou art now the blessed of the LORD.” From the lips of an outsider came the confession that God’s promise to Isaac had been fulfilled. The same blessing that had once provoked envy now commanded respect.

The irony is gentle but clear. The Philistines had tried to push Isaac away from them, and now they bind themselves to him by oath because they cannot ignore the God who is with him. Blessing, which first stirred envy, ends by drawing the outsiders near.

wordNotes.term: בְּרוּךְ יְהוָה (berukh YHWH) — the blessed of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The passive participle with the divine name means “one blessed by the LORD.” Laban used the same phrase to welcome Abraham’s servant. Its use by a foreign king confirms that God’s blessing on Isaac was evident to all, fulfilling the promise made at the start of the chapter.

Shalom denotes wholeness, safety, and right relationship rather than merely the absence of conflict. Abimelech claims to have sent Isaac away in peace, and verse 31 records that the Philistines leave Isaac in peace. The word frames the covenant as a restored relationship.

verses.bibleText: And he made them a feast, and they did eat and drink.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac answered the request with hospitality: “he made them a feast, and they did eat and drink.” In the ancient world a shared meal often sealed a covenant. Eating together expressed acceptance and mutual obligation. Jacob and Laban would later eat together on the heap of witness (31:46, 54), and Israel’s elders ate and drank before God at Sinai when the covenant was ratified (Exodus 24:11).

By hosting the meal, Isaac took the role of the stronger party extending favor. Yet the feast also displayed his generosity of spirit. The men who had hated him were now his guests. He did not make them grovel or pay. He fed them.

The scene foreshadows the gospel. God prepares a table for His people even in the presence of their enemies (Psalm 23:5), and in Christ He invites former enemies to the feast of reconciliation (Romans 5:10). Isaac’s table at Beer-sheba is a small picture of that larger generosity.

Nothing in the text suggests that Isaac exacted revenge or extracted a price for past injuries. The meal was given freely, and it was the most fitting way to show that the grievance of verse 27 had been laid aside.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun comes from the verb “to drink” and denotes a banquet or feast. Feasts marked weddings, weaning, and covenants in Genesis. Here it functions as the covenant meal, confirming the new relationship between Isaac and the Philistines.

verses.bibleText: And they rose up betimes in the morning, and sware one to another: and Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they rose up betimes in the morning, and sware one to another.” The oath was taken at the beginning of the new day, after the covenant meal. Rising early is a recurring mark of serious purpose in Genesis. Abraham rose early to obey God at Moriah (22:3), and Isaac’s guests now rose early to complete the agreement. Both parties bound themselves by oath, each accepting the obligation not to harm the other.

Then “Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace.” The language echoes Abimelech’s earlier words. He had claimed to have “sent [Isaac] away in peace” (26:29); now Isaac sends him away in peace. What the king had claimed, Isaac actually gave. The covenant ended the hostility that had marked the chapter.

The outcome justified Isaac’s policy of restraint. Had he fought at Esek or Sitnah, there might have been bloodshed and lasting enmity. Instead he yielded, and the result was a sworn peace. Jesus blessed the peacemakers and promised that they would be called the children of God (Matthew 5:9). Isaac showed the family likeness.

The oath bound both sides to the future, not only to the present moment. Isaac’s descendants would live alongside the peoples of the coastal plain for centuries, and the memory of a sworn peace at Beer-sheba belonged to the inheritance he passed on.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשָּׁבְעוּ אִישׁ לְאָחִיו (vayyishave‘u ’ish le’achiw) — and sware one to another
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “they swore, each man to his brother.” The idiom expresses mutual commitment, each party taking an oath to the other. The verb shava‘, “to swear,” is the same root that gives the well its name in verse 33.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass the same day, that Isaac's servants came, and told him concerning the well which they had digged, and said unto him, We have found water.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“It came to pass the same day” that Isaac’s servants arrived with news: “We have found water.” The timing is deliberate. On the very day the covenant was sealed, God provided a new well. Isaac had given up wells at Esek and Sitnah for the sake of peace, and now, on the day peace was secured, water came without contest.

The narrator presents this as a sign of divine approval on the covenant and on Isaac’s peaceful conduct. The God who makes room for His people also supplies their needs. The well at Beer-sheba was the reward of patience, given in a place where no one would dispute it.

The joy of the servants’ announcement echoes across Scripture. In the desert God provided water for Hagar and Ishmael (21:19) and later for Israel from the rock (Exodus 17:6). In every case the water came as a gift, not a conquest.

The report also closes a circle in the chapter. It began with famine and the threat of want; it ends, as far as Isaac’s own story is concerned, with servants arriving to say that water has been found. The God who forbade Isaac to go down to Egypt for food had sustained him in the land from first to last.

wordNotes.term: מָצָאנוּ מָיִם (matsa’nu mayim) — we have found water
wordNotes.explanation: The simple report carries the weight of relief and gratitude. In the arid south, finding water meant survival for flocks and household. The same verb “find” was used when Isaac’s servants found living water in the valley of Gerar.

verses.bibleText: And he called it Shebah: therefore the name of the city is Beer-sheba unto this day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac named the well “Shebah,” and the narrator adds, “therefore the name of the city is Beer-sheba unto this day.” The name means “oath” or “seven,” and here it clearly commemorates the oath just sworn with Abimelech. Beer-sheba means “well of the oath.”

Abraham had already given the place this name after his own covenant with an earlier Abimelech, when seven ewe lambs served as witness (21:28–31). Isaac’s naming does not contradict that earlier account. As he had done with his father’s other wells (26:18), Isaac reaffirmed the name Abraham had given, now with an added reason. A second covenant at the same place renewed the meaning of the old name. The city’s identity was thus anchored in two generations of covenant faithfulness.

The phrase “unto this day” shows that the narrator wrote for readers who still knew Beer-sheba by that name. The city would become the southern landmark of Israel’s territory, remembered in the phrase “from Dan even to Beer-sheba” (Judges 20:1). Jacob would offer sacrifices there before going down to Egypt (46:1), and Elijah would pass through it on his flight to Horeb (1 Kings 19:3).

The repeated naming teaches that God’s faithfulness to one generation is not exhausted. What He did for Abraham, He did again for Isaac at the same place. Each generation must come to know God for itself, yet it stands on a foundation laid by those who went before. Names, memorials, and well-told stories help to keep that continuity alive.

wordNotes.explanation: The name relates to the root shava‘, “to swear,” and to sheva‘, “seven.” In chapter 21 both senses meet through the seven lambs and the oath. Here the immediate association is with the oath just taken. The name links the well to the covenant it commemorates.

wordNotes.term: עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (‘ad hayyom hazzeh) — unto this day
wordNotes.explanation: The formula marks something that still existed when the account was written. It connects the narrative with the readers’ own world and confirms the lasting significance of the event. It appears often in Genesis and the historical books.

verses.bibleText: And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene turns from Isaac’s peace with outsiders to trouble within his household. “Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite.” The age is significant. Isaac had married at forty (25:20), and his father had gone to great lengths to find him a wife from among their own kin who shared their faith (24:3–4). Esau, at the same age, made his own choice without consulting his parents and took two wives at once.

The marriages broke with the family’s principles on several counts. Abraham had made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac from the daughters of Canaan (24:3). Esau married two Hittite women, outsiders to the covenant and worshipers of other gods. He also took two wives together, following the pattern of Lamech (4:19) rather than the creation pattern of one man and one woman (2:24). The narrator does not need to comment at length; the facts speak.

The notice belongs with Esau’s earlier sale of his birthright (25:29–34). The man who despised his birthright now shows the same disregard in his choice of wives. Hebrews describes Esau as a “profane person” who traded his inheritance for a single meal (Hebrews 12:16). His marriages are another expression of that profane spirit, a willingness to set aside what is sacred for what is immediately appealing.

The Hittites had been in the land since Abraham’s day; it was from Ephron the Hittite that Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah (23:10–20). Their names here are Semitic, suggesting that these families had adopted the local language. Yet they remained outside the covenant, and Esau’s alliance with them signaled his distance from the God of his fathers.

The verse also prepares for the next chapter. Esau’s unsuitability as heir of the promise is underlined just before Isaac attempts to give him the blessing. And Rebekah will use the threat of Hittite wives as a reason to send Jacob away to her family (27:46).

wordNotes.explanation: The gentilic names a people group living in Canaan in patriarchal times, counted among the nations of the land. Abraham bought his burial cave from Hittites, and Rebekah later expresses her weariness with the daughters of Heth. The term marks Esau’s wives as outsiders to the covenant family.

verses.bibleText: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter ends on a sorrowful note: Esau’s wives “were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.” The Hebrew is literally “bitterness of spirit.” These women and their ways brought lasting pain to Esau’s parents. Their foreign customs, their religion, and their attitudes clashed with the faith of Abraham’s household.

The verse names both parents. Isaac and Rebekah were about to be divided over which son should receive the blessing, yet here they share a common grief. Whatever their differences, they agreed that Esau’s marriages were a sorrow. The note is a reminder that Isaac’s favoritism toward Esau (25:28) was not based on approval of his choices.

The chapter thus closes with a contrast. Isaac had made peace with the Philistines through patience and covenant, yet within his own home a son’s choices brought bitterness. Outward success does not guarantee peace at home. Parents may do much right and still watch a child choose paths that grieve them. Proverbs speaks of a foolish son as a grief to his father and bitterness to his mother (Proverbs 17:25).

The grief also shows that the covenant family understood marriage as more than a private matter. Whom a son married affected the whole household and its relationship with God. Paul’s counsel against being unequally yoked with unbelievers (2 Corinthians 6:14) reflects the same concern. Marriage joins lives, and it can strengthen or weaken faith across generations. Grief of this kind does not cancel parental love, yet it is real, and Scripture does not hide it.

wordNotes.term: מֹרַת רוּחַ (morat ruach) — grief of mind
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means “bitterness of spirit.” The noun morah comes from the root for bitterness and describes inward anguish. The same root names Marah, the bitter waters, and appears in Naomi’s lament that the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When pressure comes, do we reach first for God’s word or for an old family strategy?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God keeps His sworn promise to Abraham through Isaac, protecting him in failure, blessing him in a hostile land, and giving him peace as he yields and worships.
discussionQuestions: What did it cost Isaac to stay in a famine-struck land rather than go down to Egypt?
What does verse 5 reveal about God’s law and its place in the life of faith before Sinai?
Why do you think Isaac repeated the very deception his father had practised?
How did Isaac’s willingness to move from disputed wells prepare the way for Rehoboth and the covenant with Abimelech?
What do Esau’s marriages show about the way small choices express the direction of a life?
commonMisunderstandings: Verse 5 does not teach that Abraham earned the covenant; his obedience was the fruit of the faith God had awakened, and the oath rested on God’s grace.
The terms for law in verse 5 do not mean God’s commandments began at Sinai; the patriarchs already knew and kept His revealed will.
Isaac’s prosperity is not a promise that faithfulness always brings wealth; the same blessing brought envy, loss of wells, and expulsion.
Isaac’s retreat from the wells was not weakness or indifference to the promise; it was trust that God would give room in His time.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Trace how God’s faithfulness, not Isaac’s performance, carries the chapter, while showing that faith takes the shape of obedience, meekness, and worship.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Stay where God has placed you, obey His voice, refuse the old strategies of fear, and trust Him to make room for you.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s sworn promise to bless the nations through Abraham’s Seed stands firm, and faith in that promise shows itself in obedience to His commandments.
flow: God swore to bless all nations through Abraham’s Seed, and He repeated that oath to Isaac.
That Seed is ultimately Christ, through whom the blessing reaches people of every nation.
Abraham received the promise by faith, and his faith showed itself in keeping God’s commandments long before Sinai.
The same God who protected Isaac in his failure offers forgiveness and room to those who come to Him.
Receiving Christ by faith leads to a life that loves and keeps God’s law.
simpleIllustrations: A well filled with earth still has water beneath it; reopening it restores what was always there, much as returning to God’s word restores a life.
A traveler who keeps stepping aside on a crowded path eventually reaches open ground; Isaac’s yielding brought him to Rehoboth.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the God of Abraham and Isaac, receive the blessing He offers in Christ, and walk in obedience to His voice?
cautions: Do not present Abraham’s obedience as the price of salvation; present it as faith’s response to grace.
Do not promise material prosperity as the sure reward of faithfulness.
Do not excuse Isaac’s deception as a clever survival tactic; Scripture records it as a failure of trust.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I tempted to go down to my own “Egypt” instead of staying where God has spoken?
Do I treat God’s commandments as a burden, or as the shape that trust takes in my life?
What fears have I inherited that lead me to protect myself at someone else’s expense?
Which disputed “well” in my life might I need to leave behind so that God can make room for me?
How might my choices today bring either joy or grief to those who have prayed for me?
